synopsis: For a program starting in October 2026, an executable SIL regression framework with machine-dynamics and braking models is realistic by mid-2027 if interfaces can be defined; how much work starts earlier depends on when the manufacturer's software can run on a computer, and sensor models may still be only partly validated [f840, f270, f65]. SIL is the economical volume-testing stage for software correctness, requirements regression and closed-loop behavior, supporting sweeps of 100+ site types and 10+ scenarios and thousands of nightly runs [f527, f925, f5266, f5267, f13327]. Its credibility depends on correlated models: it cannot independently prove production ECU timing, actual brake hardware or sensor physics in dust, snow and glare, so the recommended allocation combines SIL with HIL and whole-machine tests [f5271, f711, f5269, f5270, f5268, f13323]. HCLTech's on-road Level 3 example reports up to 75 percent less test-design effort and incremental-release validation in under a day, but discloses neither platform build time, staffing nor retained physical testing, limiting its usefulness as a planning benchmark [f1791, f1306, f1307, f1308]. Compressing validation from three or four years to under four months is credible only if the scenario library, replay adapters, SIL/HIL suites and correlated models are ready before the prototype arrives, making that period a confirmation campaign [f13085].
